name: ModuleFest Cron Monitor – Scheduled Task Control Tower
author: modulefest

sections.description:
WordPress runs scheduled work through WP-Cron, which only fires on page loads. On quiet sites tasks run late or never. On busy sites they can overlap and hammer the database. ModuleFest Cron Monitor gives you one control tower for all of it.

See what is happening

Bottleneck profiler. Every task that runs during cron is timed and measured, then ranked by duration, peak memory and failure rate. Instrumentation is attached only during real cron runs, so normal page loads are unaffected.

Health score and weekly email. One number from 0 to 100 at the top of the Dashboard, with the main reason. An optional weekly summary email sends the same to you.

Trend charts. Three 14-day charts on the Dashboard show tasks run, failed or stalled runs and the average time per task, with this week compared to the week before.

Task pages. Click any task name to open its own page: what it is, which plugin added it, its 30-day figures, charts of its recent runs and every recent run.

Per-run drill-down. See each run’s arguments, the callbacks that fired, the plugin or theme that owns them, memory, and (optionally) database query profiling.

24-hour timeline. See when every task runs over the next day, with heavy tasks and busy moments highlighted, so you can spread the load.

Update impact. After every plugin, theme or WordPress update, Cron Monitor compares that plugin’s scheduled tasks for the week before and after, and tells you if the update made them slower or start failing.

Late-task explainer. A task that is late shows why, in plain English, with a link to the fix. Common WordPress, WooCommerce and plugin tasks have friendly names and a safe-to-pause hint.

Schedule snapshots. Compare the schedule with a saved copy to see what an update added, removed or changed. One is taken automatically before any update.

Action Scheduler insights. If WooCommerce or another plugin uses Action Scheduler, see its queue next to WP-Cron: past-due and failed actions, 14-day charts, which actions fail most and how much database space the queue uses, and tidy up old finished actions in one click.

WordPress Dashboard box and CSV export. See the health score on the main WordPress Dashboard, and export run history as a spreadsheet.

Get warned before it matters

Stall recovery and alerts. A shutdown guard, active only during cron runs, records fatal errors mid-task. Tasks that run past your stall threshold are closed and, if recurring, rescheduled. Email and chat alerts are rate-limited so you are never flooded.

Stopped-task warnings. When a repeating task stops running, or falls far behind, Cron Monitor says so on the Dashboard and in Health Check, sends one alert and includes it in the weekly email. A silent backup that stopped last Tuesday no longer goes unnoticed.

Slowing-task warnings. When a task starts taking at least three times as long as usual, Cron Monitor tells you before it starts timing out.

Watch a task and alert history. Set your own alert rules on important tasks, and see every alert Cron Monitor has sent, or held back and why.

Alerts as Slack, Teams, Discord and Google Chat cards. Alerts arrive as a proper card with the task, the site and a button back to Cron Monitor. The service is worked out from the webhook address.

Outside check-ins. A site that is down cannot warn anyone itself. Turn on check-ins and the site reports to a watchtower (another site running Cron Monitor, such as your agency’s) every few minutes; the watchtower alerts you when a site stops checking in, and when it is back.

Fix problems in one click

One-click fixes. Health › Fix problems finds a stuck cron lock, repeating tasks scheduled twice, tasks on a schedule that no longer exists, missed runs and busy moments, and fixes each with one button. Changes to your task list can be undone for a day.

Leftover-task clean-up. Plugins you switched off or deleted often leave scheduled tasks behind that wake cron for nothing. Cron Monitor lists them, says which plugin they probably came from, and removes them with one click.

Overlap protection. Mark heavy tasks as “guarded” and only one copy will run at a time. An overlapping copy is skipped and retried shortly after, so no work is lost.

Event editor. Reschedule, re-time, pause, resume, add and remove events, and manage custom schedules.

Quiet hours. Keep backups, imports and other heavy tasks to a quiet time of night.

Maintenance pause. Hold every scheduled task while you deploy or migrate, then resume and catch up in one click.

Test my cron. One button checks a task really runs on time, and explains what to fix if it does not.

Run cron on time

Real cron trigger. A secret REST endpoint lets a server crontab or an uptime monitor run cron on an exact schedule. An optional, throttled loopback keepalive helps sites that still get some traffic. The plugin never edits wp-config.php: switching off the page-load trigger (DISABLE_WP_CRON) is your choice, and the Setup Wizard shows you exactly what to add.

Server cron in one click. On cPanel hosting, connect with an API token and Cron Monitor creates the server cron job for you, then shows the last step to finish.

For agencies and networks

For agencies. Each client site can switch on a read-only status link with a secret key. Add those sites to the Agency overview on your own site to see every client’s health in one grid, get one alert when a client needs attention or cannot be reached (and one when it recovers), put the client’s name on every alert and summary, print or save a one-page client report, and send the client a read-only status page.

Multisite networks. Network-activate it and one real cron trigger on the main site runs due tasks on every site in the network, so quiet sites never miss their tasks. Network Admin shows every site’s health score, late tasks, failures and last run in one list, least healthy first. Set alert email, webhook, stall threshold and more once for the whole network (and lock them if you like), and get one weekly summary for the network instead of one email per site.

Works with other ModuleFest tools. Install Disk Space Manager or Memory Manager as well and they join up with Cron Monitor: one menu bar, a card from each on the Dashboard, one set of alert settings and one weekly email. Each still works fully on its own.

WP-CLI. wp cronmonitor list|run|pause|resume|profile|history|health|purge for agencies managing many sites. On a network, health --network and run --network cover every site at once.

Also included: a guided Setup Wizard, an on-demand Health Check, a KPI dashboard, contextual Help tabs on every screen, and a Help & Guide page with step-by-step walkthroughs, an FAQ and a glossary.

Everything here is free. Every feature is available from the moment you activate it, with no time limit and no account. Everything runs on your own site.

Formerly Cron-Sentry. If you used Cron-Sentry, activating this plugin imports your settings, paused tasks, custom schedules and run history. A notice then reminds you to deactivate and delete Cron-Sentry.

More from ModuleFest

Cron Monitor is made by ModuleFest. Our other free plugins on WordPress.org:

  • ModuleFest Pet Groomer – bookings, clients, pets and a staff app for grooming businesses.
  • ModuleFest Pet Walker – walks, clients, pets and a staff app for dog-walking businesses.

Guides for every Cron Monitor feature are at modulefest.com/help/cronmonitor. You can also ask for Cron Monitor news by email from the plugin’s Dashboard; nothing is sent unless you choose to subscribe.

External services

This plugin makes outgoing requests only in the cases below. Nothing is sent on activation.

Chat webhook (optional, off until you enter a URL). If you enter a webhook URL under Settings → Alerts, the plugin sends a POST request to that URL when a task errors, stalls, stops or breaks a rule you set (rate-limited per task), when a watched site stops or starts checking in, when a client site on your Agency overview needs attention, and when you click “Send test alert”. For Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord and Google Chat addresses the message is a formatted card; any other address receives plain JSON. It contains the alert type, the task name, a short message, your site’s address and name, the time and a link back to Cron Monitor. The service receiving it is the one you choose, so its own terms and privacy policy apply.

Outside check-ins (optional, off by default). If you tick “Check in with a watchtower” under Settings → Outside check-ins, the plugin sends a POST request every 5 to 60 minutes (your choice) to the watchtower address you enter, which is another site running Cron Monitor that you or your agency control. It sends this site’s address and name, its health score, the number of late tasks, the Cron Monitor version and whether a maintenance pause is on, with the check-in key you entered. Nothing is sent to ModuleFest.

cPanel (optional, only when you connect it). If you connect cPanel under Health → Server cron, the plugin calls the cPanel server you enter (its JSON API on port 2083 by default) with the username and API token you enter, only to list, add and remove this site’s cron job when you open that screen or press its buttons. The token is stored in this site’s database and removed when you press Disconnect.

Alert email (optional). Alerts are sent with WordPress’s own wp_mail() to the address you enter, or to the site admin email if you leave it blank, through whatever mail setup your site already uses. The email contains the same details as the chat alert.

Your own site (loopback). The keepalive, the “Test trigger” button and the Health Check make requests to your own site (wp-cron.php and the REST API). Nothing leaves your server unless your site’s URL points elsewhere.

ModuleFest newsletter sign-up (support.modulefest.com, only when you press Subscribe). The Dashboard and the About ModuleFest screen show a “Get news for Cron Monitor” card. Only when you tick its consent box and press Subscribe does the plugin send one request to https://support.modulefest.com/wp-json/modulefest/v1/subscribe. It sends the name and email you entered, this site’s address, the plugin’s name and version, and the consent wording you agreed to, so that ModuleFest can send you the newsletter you asked for. ModuleFest then emails you to confirm, and every email has a link to change or leave. The plugin does not store your email address, and no feature depends on subscribing. Privacy policy · Terms of service.

WordPress.org plugin details (only when you click). The About ModuleFest screen lists other free ModuleFest plugins. Clicking “View details” opens WordPress’s own plugin window, and WordPress itself fetches that listing from WordPress.org (api.wordpress.org). Nothing is fetched until you click. WordPress.org privacy policy.

External cron services (your choice). If you use an outside uptime monitor or cron service to call your trigger URL, that service calls your site; the plugin does not contact it. Its own terms apply.

Source code

There is no build step. The PHP, JavaScript (assets/admin.js) and CSS (assets/admin.css) in this plugin are the source, shipped unminified with their comments. The plugin bundles no third-party libraries.
sections.installation:
1. In wp-admin go to Plugins → Add New, search for “ModuleFest Cron Monitor”, then install and activate it. Or upload the modulefest-cron-monitor folder to /wp-content/plugins/ and activate it.
  2. You are taken to the Setup Wizard. Choose your cron mode, guard heavy tasks, set up alerts and, if you like, the keepalive.
  3. Run the Health Check (Cron Monitor → Health Check) any time to confirm everything is green.

For the most reliable timing, add define( 'DISABLE_WP_CRON', true ); to wp-config.php yourself and call the trigger URL from a real crontab or uptime monitor every 1–5 minutes. The wizard and Settings page show the exact URL and crontab line.
sections.faq:
Does profiling slow down my site?

No. Instrumentation is attached only while WordPress is running cron, so normal front-end and admin requests carry no profiling overhead. Database query profiling is off by default.

Will guarding a task make it run less often?

Only when a previous run has not finished. The overlapping copy is skipped and retried shortly after.

Can this create traffic on a site with no visitors?

No plugin can. Use the real cron trigger with a server crontab or an uptime monitor. The wizard walks you through it.

Is the cron trigger URL safe to use?

Yes. It only runs cron when the request carries your site’s secret key, checked in constant time. You can rotate the key at any time under Settings; remember to update your crontab or monitor afterwards.

Does the plugin change wp-config.php or turn off WP-Cron?

No. It only shows you the line to add if you choose to.

Does it send any data anywhere?

Only what you choose: alert emails to the address you enter (or your site admin email if you leave it blank), chat alerts to the webhook you enter, outside check-ins to the watchtower address you enter (off until you switch them on), calls to your own cPanel server when you connect it under Server cron, and, if you press Subscribe on the “Get news for Cron Monitor” card, your sign-up to the ModuleFest newsletter. Nothing is sent on activation, and nothing is ever sent to ModuleFest in the background. See External services below.

The optional Agency status link is off by default. When a site owner switches it on, the site answers requests to its status address that carry its secret key, with scheduled-task health only (score, late tasks, failure counts, Cron Monitor and WordPress versions). It sends nothing by itself. An agency site that adds client sites requests those addresses in the background every 15 minutes.

What happens when I delete the plugin?

Deactivating keeps your history and settings. Deleting the plugin removes its log table, options, transients and its own maintenance task (on a multisite network, from every site). It never touches other plugins’ scheduled events; anything you had paused simply resumes.

I used Cron-Sentry. What changes?

Your settings and history are imported automatically when you activate this plugin. Then deactivate and delete Cron-Sentry on the Plugins page. The trigger URL changes to /wp-json/mfcs/v1/run?key=…, so update your crontab or monitor; a notice shows the new URL. The WP-CLI command is now wp cronmonitor.

Are there other ModuleFest plugins?

Yes. See all our free plugins on our WordPress.org profile, or visit modulefest.com. The plugin’s About page lists them too.

What are the Welcome and What’s new windows?

A short Welcome window appears once per site, the first time someone opens a Cron Monitor screen on a new install. After each update, a What’s new window lists the changes once per person. They appear only on Cron Monitor’s own screens, close for good with one press, and contact no other site.

Where do I get help?

Use the plugin’s support forum on WordPress.org. The plugin also has a Help & Guide page and contextual Help tabs on every screen.

short_description: Watch every WordPress scheduled task: health score, trend charts, alerts in email or chat, one-click fixes and a real cron trigger.
description:
WordPress runs scheduled work through WP-Cron, which only fires on page loads. On quiet sites tasks run late or never. On busy sites they can overlap and hammer the database. ModuleFest Cron Monitor gives you one control tower for all of it.

See what is happening

Bottleneck profiler. Every task that runs during cron is timed and measured, then ranked by duration, peak memory and failure rate. Instrumentation is attached only during real cron runs, so normal page loads are unaffected.

Health score and weekly email. One number from 0 to 100 at the top of the Dashboard, with the main reason. An optional weekly summary email sends the same to you.

Trend charts. Three 14-day charts on the Dashboard show tasks run, failed or stalled runs and the average time per task, with this week compared to the week before.

Task pages. Click any task name to open its own page: what it is, which plugin added it, its 30-day figures, charts of its recent runs and every recent run.

Per-run drill-down. See each run’s arguments, the callbacks that fired, the plugin or theme that owns them, memory, and (optionally) database query profiling.

24-hour timeline. See when every task runs over the next day, with heavy tasks and busy moments highlighted, so you can spread the load.

Update impact. After every plugin, theme or WordPress update, Cron Monitor compares that plugin’s scheduled tasks for the week before and after, and tells you if the update made them slower or start failing.

Late-task explainer. A task that is late shows why, in plain English, with a link to the fix. Common WordPress, WooCommerce and plugin tasks have friendly names and a safe-to-pause hint.

Schedule snapshots. Compare the schedule with a saved copy to see what an update added, removed or changed. One is taken automatically before any update.

Action Scheduler insights. If WooCommerce or another plugin uses Action Scheduler, see its queue next to WP-Cron: past-due and failed actions, 14-day charts, which actions fail most and how much database space the queue uses, and tidy up old finished actions in one click.

WordPress Dashboard box and CSV export. See the health score on the main WordPress Dashboard, and export run history as a spreadsheet.

Get warned before it matters

Stall recovery and alerts. A shutdown guard, active only during cron runs, records fatal errors mid-task. Tasks that run past your stall threshold are closed and, if recurring, rescheduled. Email and chat alerts are rate-limited so you are never flooded.

Stopped-task warnings. When a repeating task stops running, or falls far behind, Cron Monitor says so on the Dashboard and in Health Check, sends one alert and includes it in the weekly email. A silent backup that stopped last Tuesday no longer goes unnoticed.

Slowing-task warnings. When a task starts taking at least three times as long as usual, Cron Monitor tells you before it starts timing out.

Watch a task and alert history. Set your own alert rules on important tasks, and see every alert Cron Monitor has sent, or held back and why.

Alerts as Slack, Teams, Discord and Google Chat cards. Alerts arrive as a proper card with the task, the site and a button back to Cron Monitor. The service is worked out from the webhook address.

Outside check-ins. A site that is down cannot warn anyone itself. Turn on check-ins and the site reports to a watchtower (another site running Cron Monitor, such as your agency’s) every few minutes; the watchtower alerts you when a site stops checking in, and when it is back.

Fix problems in one click

One-click fixes. Health › Fix problems finds a stuck cron lock, repeating tasks scheduled twice, tasks on a schedule that no longer exists, missed runs and busy moments, and fixes each with one button. Changes to your task list can be undone for a day.

Leftover-task clean-up. Plugins you switched off or deleted often leave scheduled tasks behind that wake cron for nothing. Cron Monitor lists them, says which plugin they probably came from, and removes them with one click.

Overlap protection. Mark heavy tasks as “guarded” and only one copy will run at a time. An overlapping copy is skipped and retried shortly after, so no work is lost.

Event editor. Reschedule, re-time, pause, resume, add and remove events, and manage custom schedules.

Quiet hours. Keep backups, imports and other heavy tasks to a quiet time of night.

Maintenance pause. Hold every scheduled task while you deploy or migrate, then resume and catch up in one click.

Test my cron. One button checks a task really runs on time, and explains what to fix if it does not.

Run cron on time

Real cron trigger. A secret REST endpoint lets a server crontab or an uptime monitor run cron on an exact schedule. An optional, throttled loopback keepalive helps sites that still get some traffic. The plugin never edits wp-config.php: switching off the page-load trigger (DISABLE_WP_CRON) is your choice, and the Setup Wizard shows you exactly what to add.

Server cron in one click. On cPanel hosting, connect with an API token and Cron Monitor creates the server cron job for you, then shows the last step to finish.

For agencies and networks

For agencies. Each client site can switch on a read-only status link with a secret key. Add those sites to the Agency overview on your own site to see every client’s health in one grid, get one alert when a client needs attention or cannot be reached (and one when it recovers), put the client’s name on every alert and summary, print or save a one-page client report, and send the client a read-only status page.

Multisite networks. Network-activate it and one real cron trigger on the main site runs due tasks on every site in the network, so quiet sites never miss their tasks. Network Admin shows every site’s health score, late tasks, failures and last run in one list, least healthy first. Set alert email, webhook, stall threshold and more once for the whole network (and lock them if you like), and get one weekly summary for the network instead of one email per site.

Works with other ModuleFest tools. Install Disk Space Manager or Memory Manager as well and they join up with Cron Monitor: one menu bar, a card from each on the Dashboard, one set of alert settings and one weekly email. Each still works fully on its own.

WP-CLI. wp cronmonitor list|run|pause|resume|profile|history|health|purge for agencies managing many sites. On a network, health --network and run --network cover every site at once.

Also included: a guided Setup Wizard, an on-demand Health Check, a KPI dashboard, contextual Help tabs on every screen, and a Help & Guide page with step-by-step walkthroughs, an FAQ and a glossary.

Everything here is free. Every feature is available from the moment you activate it, with no time limit and no account. Everything runs on your own site.

Formerly Cron-Sentry. If you used Cron-Sentry, activating this plugin imports your settings, paused tasks, custom schedules and run history. A notice then reminds you to deactivate and delete Cron-Sentry.

More from ModuleFest

Cron Monitor is made by ModuleFest. Our other free plugins on WordPress.org:

  • ModuleFest Pet Groomer – bookings, clients, pets and a staff app for grooming businesses.
  • ModuleFest Pet Walker – walks, clients, pets and a staff app for dog-walking businesses.

Guides for every Cron Monitor feature are at modulefest.com/help/cronmonitor. You can also ask for Cron Monitor news by email from the plugin’s Dashboard; nothing is sent unless you choose to subscribe.

External services

This plugin makes outgoing requests only in the cases below. Nothing is sent on activation.

Chat webhook (optional, off until you enter a URL). If you enter a webhook URL under Settings → Alerts, the plugin sends a POST request to that URL when a task errors, stalls, stops or breaks a rule you set (rate-limited per task), when a watched site stops or starts checking in, when a client site on your Agency overview needs attention, and when you click “Send test alert”. For Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord and Google Chat addresses the message is a formatted card; any other address receives plain JSON. It contains the alert type, the task name, a short message, your site’s address and name, the time and a link back to Cron Monitor. The service receiving it is the one you choose, so its own terms and privacy policy apply.

Outside check-ins (optional, off by default). If you tick “Check in with a watchtower” under Settings → Outside check-ins, the plugin sends a POST request every 5 to 60 minutes (your choice) to the watchtower address you enter, which is another site running Cron Monitor that you or your agency control. It sends this site’s address and name, its health score, the number of late tasks, the Cron Monitor version and whether a maintenance pause is on, with the check-in key you entered. Nothing is sent to ModuleFest.

cPanel (optional, only when you connect it). If you connect cPanel under Health → Server cron, the plugin calls the cPanel server you enter (its JSON API on port 2083 by default) with the username and API token you enter, only to list, add and remove this site’s cron job when you open that screen or press its buttons. The token is stored in this site’s database and removed when you press Disconnect.

Alert email (optional). Alerts are sent with WordPress’s own wp_mail() to the address you enter, or to the site admin email if you leave it blank, through whatever mail setup your site already uses. The email contains the same details as the chat alert.

Your own site (loopback). The keepalive, the “Test trigger” button and the Health Check make requests to your own site (wp-cron.php and the REST API). Nothing leaves your server unless your site’s URL points elsewhere.

ModuleFest newsletter sign-up (support.modulefest.com, only when you press Subscribe). The Dashboard and the About ModuleFest screen show a “Get news for Cron Monitor” card. Only when you tick its consent box and press Subscribe does the plugin send one request to https://support.modulefest.com/wp-json/modulefest/v1/subscribe. It sends the name and email you entered, this site’s address, the plugin’s name and version, and the consent wording you agreed to, so that ModuleFest can send you the newsletter you asked for. ModuleFest then emails you to confirm, and every email has a link to change or leave. The plugin does not store your email address, and no feature depends on subscribing. Privacy policy · Terms of service.

WordPress.org plugin details (only when you click). The About ModuleFest screen lists other free ModuleFest plugins. Clicking “View details” opens WordPress’s own plugin window, and WordPress itself fetches that listing from WordPress.org (api.wordpress.org). Nothing is fetched until you click. WordPress.org privacy policy.

External cron services (your choice). If you use an outside uptime monitor or cron service to call your trigger URL, that service calls your site; the plugin does not contact it. Its own terms apply.

Source code

There is no build step. The PHP, JavaScript (assets/admin.js) and CSS (assets/admin.css) in this plugin are the source, shipped unminified with their comments. The plugin bundles no third-party libraries.

screenshots.caption: Dashboard: health score, a warning when a task gets slower, 14-day trend charts and the last 24 hours at a glance.
Task page: one task's figures, its own alert rules, and charts of the time and memory of its recent runs.
Timeline: when every task runs over the next 24 hours, with heavy tasks and busy moments marked.
Health Check: Test my cron plus pass and warning checks, each with a link to the fix.
Fix problems: common scheduled-task problems fixed in one click, with undo.
Update impact: each plugin update's tasks compared for the week before and after.
Alert history: every alert sent or held back, by email and chat, with the reason.
Watchtower: sites that check in from outside, and an alert when one goes quiet.
